nba_directive.reason_text: This client is waiting on the Fed before acting, but mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury — not the Fed funds rate — so anticipated cuts are likely already priced in; delivering that education is the highest-leverage move for a rate-threshold client and converts at ~2.4x the odds of a soft pull. With a 2.25% first mortgage, a cash-out refi would be destructive, so any equity conversation must be framed as a HELOC that leaves the first untouched.
nba_directive.recommended_strategy_text:
- Lead with the Fed-vs-mortgage education before anything else
  - Open exactly: 'Quick thing worth knowing — mortgage rates don't actually follow the Fed rate. They track the 10-year Treasury, and any cuts the Fed is expected to make are already baked into today's mortgage pricing. So waiting for a Fed move may not move your rate the way you're thinking.'
  - This reframe is the door-opener; do not skip it or bury it

- Pivot immediately to their specific rate threshold with real math
  - Their current P&I is $2,293/mo on a $227,706 remaining balance at 2.25%
  - Ask them directly: 'What rate would make this worth doing for you?' — get the number on record
  - Once you have their target rate, run the actual P&I at that rate on their remaining balance and show the monthly delta in dollars
  - Carry a break-even: divide closing cost estimate by monthly savings to show the month they come out ahead — present this as a concrete timeline, not a vague promise

- Protect the 2.25% first mortgage — do NOT pitch a cash-out refi
  - If they have equity needs or high-rate debt, frame a HELOC / second lien as the tool that leaves the 2.25% untouched
  - Reframe the HELOC rate against credit-card rates (25–30%): even a higher second-lien rate is a steep discount to revolving debt
  - If they share any balances, run the actual monthly interest they're paying on that debt vs. what a HELOC payment would be — let the spread do the work

- Anchor to their specific financial pain, not a generic rate pitch
  - Ask one clarifying question: 'What's the main thing you're trying to accomplish — lower the payment, pay off other debt, or something else?' — then reframe the loan as solving that named problem
  - Tie every number back to their $2,293/mo baseline so the comparison is concrete

- Secure the next step before ending the text thread
  - Offer a 10-minute call to run the live numbers together, or send a soft-pull authorization link so you can pull a real scenario
  - Do not close with an open-ended 'let me know' — give them a specific choice: 'Want me to text you the break-even calc, or easier to do a quick call?'
